deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (from the previous page). For complex p=x+iy and p'=x'+iy' with y, y' >= 0 and x' > x, Gauss defines [p,p'] as the number of lattice points (X,Y) with x < X <= x' and 0 < Y <= the ordinate of the segment from p to p' at abscissa X. In words, it counts the lattice points under the chord p->p' and above the real axis, with the left edge open and the right edge closed. He sets [p,p']=0 if x'=x and [p,p']=-[p',p] if x'<x. Here a bracket of a single real number, [x], is the integer part floor(x), as in the Disquisitiones. The count of integer X in (x,x'] is [x']-[x].

TOP OF THIS PAGE (end of section 3). If y or y' is negative, choose an integer n with y+n>0 and y'+n>0 and put [p,p'] := [p+in, p'+in] - n[x'] + n[x]. The manuscript writes the second argument as 'p+in''; read p'+in.
- Justification (mine): raising the segment by n adds exactly n lattice points in each of the [x']-[x] admissible columns.
- So the right-hand side does not depend on n, as Gauss says. The quantity is now defined for all p, p'.

SECTION 4. Four 'self-evident' theorems, for p=x+iy, p'=x'+iy' and n an integer.
- I. [p+ni, p'+ni] = [p,p'] - n[x'] + n[x]. This is a vertical-translation rule. As written the sign is reversed; see errors.
- II. [p+n, p'+n] = [p,p']. The lattice is invariant under integer horizontal translation.
- III. If (p''-p')/(p'-p) is real, i.e. p, p', p'' are collinear, then [p,p''] = [p,p'] + [p',p''], 'and so for any number of points'. This is additivity of the signed count along subdivisions of one line, made possible by the antisymmetry convention.
- IV. Let P=a+ib be a Gaussian integer, with p/P = m+in and p'/P = m'+in' (m, n, m', n' real; n is reused). Then [p,p'] = [p,mP] + [mP,m'P] + [m'P,p'] + sum over alpha of [(alpha+p)/P, (alpha+p')/P], alpha running over the 'least residues' modulo P.

My reading of IV:
- [p,p'] - [p,mP] - [mP,m'P] - [m'P,p'] is the signed count of Gaussian integers z in the quadrilateral p, p', m'P, mP. This is the region under the chord p p', measured from the line R*P in the direction iP.
- Write every Gaussian integer uniquely as z = Pw - alpha, with w in Z[i] and alpha a residue mod P.
- Then z lies in the quadrilateral iff w lies in the region under the chord (alpha+p)/P -> (alpha+p')/P and above the horizontal line Im w = Im(alpha/P).
- This differs from [(alpha+p)/P, (alpha+p')/P] by the count of lattice points between Im w = 0 and Im w = Im(alpha/P).
- That difference vanishes when the residues are taken with 0 <= Im(alpha/P) < 1, apart from boundary conventions.
- So IV is a reduction formula: lattice counts under complex chords are transformed by a Gaussian-integer modulus, in the spirit of Gauss's third proof of quadratic reciprocity. The next page is headed 'Die biquadratischen Reste', so this serves biquadratic reciprocity.

LOWER PART (scratch). This uses the half-unit bracket defined on the next page: [x] = x for integer x and floor(x)+1/2 otherwise, extended so that [-x] = -[x]. Equivalently [x] = (floor x + ceil x)/2.
- Gauss tests the multiplication formula [mx] = [x] + [x+1/m] + ... + [x+(m-1)/m], and finds the correction -(m-1)/2.
- Example 1, x=1/3, m=6. The arguments 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 5/6, 1, 7/6 have brackets 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1/2, 1, 3/2. The sum is 9/2, and 9/2 - 5/2 = 2 = [2] = [6*(1/3)].
- Example 2, x=-1/2, m=6. The arguments 1/3, 1/6, 0, -1/6, -1/3, -1/2 have brackets 1/2, 1/2, 0, -1/2, -1/2, -1/2. The sum is -1/2, and -1/2 - 5/2 = -3 = [-3].
- Example 3, x=3.7, m=4, mx=14.8. The integers 1..14 are tabulated by residue mod 4: rows {4,8,12}, {1,5,9,13}, {2,6,10,14}, {3,7,11}, with counts 3, 4, 4, 3.
- Adding 1/2 for the endpoint 0 gives the total [14.8] = 14 1/2.
- The second column gives [3.7]=3.5, [3.45]=3.5, [3.2]=3.5, [2.95]=2.5, i.e. [x - r/4] for r = 0..3. These sum to 13, and 13 + 3/2 = 14.5 = [14.8].
- So this is the same identity, in the form [mx] = sum over r of [x - r/m] + (m-1)/2.

The abbreviations 'L.L.f.B / f.b.i.d.v.u.b.' and the sketch of a triangle with an altitude whose foot is extended by dotted lines appear unrelated to the mathematics.
errors: The definition line has 'p+in'' as the second argument; it must be p'+in, otherwise x' and the n[x'] term would not match.
Theorem I has the sign reversed. The definition just above gives [p+ni,p'+ni] = [p,p'] + n[x'] - n[x]. The written form '[p+ni,p'+ni] = [p,p'] - n[x'] + n[x]' is valid only with n replaced by -n.

Theorem IV needs a particular residue system (e.g. 0 <= Im(alpha/P) < 1) and care with open/closed boundaries along the sides parallel to iP. Otherwise extra terms [(alpha+mP)/P, (alpha+m'P)/P] appear. 'Kleinste Reste' is not specified precisely enough, so the statement is only correct under suitable conventions.
Notation clash in IV: n is used both for the integer of Theorem I and for the imaginary part of p/P.
The scratch identities are numerically correct. The correction -(m-1)/2 is necessary for the half-unit bracket; it vanishes for the floor function (Hermite's identity).

results.what: Signed lattice-point count [p,p'] under the chord between two complex numbers, extended to arbitrary positions by translation and antisymmetry; translation laws I and II and collinear additivity III
results.modern_name: Lattice-point (Eisenstein-type) counting under a segment; Dedekind-sum-like floor sums
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844, geometric lattice-point form of Gauss's third proof); Gauss for the underlying floor-sum lemma (1808)

results.what: Reduction of the lattice count modulo a Gaussian integer P: [p,p'] equals boundary terms plus the sum over residues alpha of [(alpha+p)/P, (alpha+p')/P]
results.modern_name: Lattice-point / Gauss-lemma approach to biquadratic (quartic) reciprocity over Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844-50) for proofs of biquadratic reciprocity; Gauss's Nachlass fragments on biquadratic residues

results.what: Multiplication formula for the half-unit bracket: [mx] = sum_{k=0}^{m-1} [x+k/m] - (m-1)/2
results.modern_name: Hermite's identity (variant for the symmetric floor (floor+ceil)/2)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's unpublished work on biquadratic reciprocity, including half-unit brackets and lattice counts, is known in outline from Werke II. The explicit complex-endpoint lattice count, with a reduction formula modulo a Gaussian integer, is a notable unpublished detail anticipating Eisenstein-style geometric arguments, but it is not a major unknown result. The Hermite-type identity is a minor scratch check.
